claim: ACE2 is a major cell entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2
source: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) is a major cell entry receptor for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction

claim: Using 45 different luciferase reporters, the transcription factors SP1 and HNF4α were found to positively and negatively regulate ACE2 expression, respectively, at the transcriptional level in human lung epithelial cells (HPAEpiCs)
source: Using 45 different luciferase reporters, the transcription factors SP1 and HNF4α were found to positively and negatively regulate ACE2 expression, respectively, at the transcriptional level in human lung epithelial cells (HPAEpiCs).
evidence: This finding is based on experimental data using the Cignal Finder 45-Pathway Reporter Array as described in the methods and results

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection increased the transcriptional activity of SP1 while inhibiting that of HNF4α
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection increased the transcriptional activity of SP1 while inhibiting that of HNF4α.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased SP1 phosphorylation and cytoplasmic translocation of HNF4α upon SARS-CoV-2 infection

claim: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, activated by SARS-CoV-2 infection, served as a crucial regulatory node, inducing ACE2 expression by enhancing SP1 phosphorylation and reducing the nuclear localization of HNF4α
source: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, activated by SARS-CoV-2 infection, served as a crucial regulatory node, inducing ACE2 expression by enhancing SP1 phosphorylation—a marker of its activity—and reducing the nuclear localization of HNF4α.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing AKT phosphorylation upon SARS-CoV-2 infection and effects of PI3K inhibitors on ACE2 expression

claim: Colchicine treatment inhibited the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, thereby suppressing ACE2 expression
source: However, colchicine treatment inhibited the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, thereby suppressing ACE2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced AKT phosphorylation and ACE2 expression upon colchicine treatment

claim: In Syrian hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2, inhibition of SP1 by either mithramycin A or colchicine resulted in reduced viral replication and tissue injury
source: In Syrian hamsters (Mesocricetus auratus) infected with SARS-CoV-2, inhibition of SP1 by either mithramycin A or colchicine resulted in reduced viral replication and tissue injury.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data in Syrian hamsters showing reduced viral loads and histopathological damage

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is the causative pathogen of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic
source: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) is the causative pathogen of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic (Wu et al., 2020; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: Patients with severe COVID-19 often exhibit pathophysiological characteristics related to a systemic inflammatory response, manifesting as acute respiratory distress syndrome and multiorgan dysfunction
source: Patients with severe COVID-19 often exhibit pathophysiological characteristics related to a systemic inflammatory response, manifesting as acute respiratory distress syndrome and multiorgan dysfunction (Pan et al., 2021; van Eijk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: Viral entry into host cells occurs through the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to its cellular receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), followed by proteolytic cleavage of the spike protein via the transmembrane serine protease TMPRSS2
source: Viral entry into host cells occurs through the binding of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein to its cellular receptor, angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), followed by proteolytic cleavage of the spike protein via the transmembrane serine protease TMPRSS2 (Yan et al., 2020), facilitating the fusion of the viral and host cell membranes, a crucial step for viral internalization (Hoffmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: ACE2 is widely expressed in different human tissues, including the lungs, small intestine, kidneys, liver, testes, heart, and brain
source: ACE2 is widely expressed in different human tissues, including the lungs, small intestine, kidneys, liver, testes, heart, and brain (Dong et al., 2020; Verdecchia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: The widespread expression of ACE2 may account for the multi-organ targeting observed with SARS-CoV-2
source: Such widespread expression of ACE2 may account for the multi-organ targeting observed with SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known expression pattern of ACE2 and clinical observations

claim: The efficacy of existing vaccines has shown a marked decline against emergent variants such as Omicron
source: Notably, the efficacy of existing vaccines has shown a marked decline against emergent variants such as Omicron (Kuhlmann et al., 2022; Wilhelm et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: Modifications in the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 variants have been observed to increase their binding affinity to ACE2, thereby enhancing transmissibility
source: Modifications in the spike protein of these variants have been observed to increase their binding affinity to ACE2, thereby enhancing transmissibility (Liu et al., 2021; McCallum et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly up-regulates ACE2 expression
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that SARS-CoV-2 infection significantly up-regulates ACE2 expression (Gao et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021a; Zhuang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by experimental data in this study

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection can increase the expression of HMGB1, which subsequently induces the expression of ACE2, possibly through an epigenetic mechanism
source: Specifically, SARS-CoV-2 infection can increase the expression of HMGB1, which subsequently induces the expression of ACE2, possibly through an epigenetic mechanism (Wei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Overexpression of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein markedly up-regulates ACE2 expression, a process reliant on type I interferon signaling pathways, with ACE2 being identified as an interferon-stimulated gene
source: Furthermore, overexpression of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein markedly up-regulates ACE2 expression, a process reliant on type I interferon signaling pathways, with ACE2 being identified as an interferon-stimulated gene (Zhou et al., 2021; Ziegler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: The androgen receptor positively regulates the expression of ACE2 at the transcriptional level
source: Several studies have demonstrated that the androgen receptor positively regulates the expression of ACE2 at the transcriptional level (Qiao et al., 2021; Samuel et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: Attenuation of ACE2 expression via suppression of the androgen receptor signaling decreases SARS-CoV-2 infectivity
source: Importantly, attenuation of ACE2 expression via suppression of the androgen receptor signaling decreases SARS-CoV-2 infectivity (Qiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), an inhibitor of the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), reduces ACE2 expression in human lung, intestinal, and liver organoids, thereby inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 infection
source: Recent research has also demonstrated that ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), an inhibitor of the farnesoid X receptor (FXR), reduces ACE2 expression in human lung, intestinal, and liver organoids, thereby inhibiting SARS-CoV-2 infection (Brevini et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection up-regulated ACE2 protein expression in HPAEpiCs
source: Consistent with prior studies indicating a significant up-regulation of ACE2 mRNA expression following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Gao et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2021b; Zhuang et al., 2020), we found that SARS-CoV-2 infection up-regulated ACE2 protein expression in HPAEpiCs, a human lung epithelial cell line (Figure 1A, B), with further corroboration based on immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 1C, D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior research

claim: Colchicine treatment substantially inhibited ACE2 expression in HPAEpiCs, irrespective of SARS-CoV-2 infection status
source: In the present study, we observed that colchicine treatment substantially inhibited ACE2 expression in HPAEpiCs, irrespective of SARS-CoV-2 infection status (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Colchicine treatment reduced extracellular SARS-CoV-2 replication in HPAEpiCs
source: Based on quantitative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), colchicine treatment reduced extracellular SARS-CoV-2 replication in cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of colchicine for inhibiting viral replication was 0.2703 μM
source: The half-maximal effective concentration (EC50) of colchicine for inhibiting viral replication was 0.2703 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Three transcription factors (SP1, NF-κB, and GATA) were enhanced by SARS-CoV-2 infection and suppressed by colchicine treatment
source: Among the tested signaling pathways, three transcription factors (SP1, NF-κB, and GATA) enhanced by SARS-CoV-2 infection and suppressed by colchicine treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Cignal Finder 45-Pathway Reporter Array shown in Figure 2A

claim: Two signaling pathways (HNF4α and estrogen receptor) were inactivated by SARS-CoV-2 infection but activated by colchicine treatment
source: Conversely, two signaling pathways (HNF4α and estrogen receptor) were inactivated by SARS-CoV-2 infection but activated by colchicine treatment (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the Cignal Finder 45-Pathway Reporter Array shown in Figure 2A

claim: Two significantly enriched motifs were found 1.5 kb upstream of the transcription start site of the ACE2 gene, annotated as the motifs of the transcription factors SP1 (p=6.1e-5) and HNF4α (p=4.2e-5)
source: Our analysis revealed two significantly enriched motifs (Figure 2B), annotated as the motifs of the transcription factors SP1 (p=6.1e-5) and HNF4α (p=4.2e-5).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis using the MEME program shown in Figure 2B

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection markedly increased the phosphorylation levels of SP1 at Thr453
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection markedly increased the phosphorylation levels of SP1 at Thr453, whereas colchicine treatment significantly inhibited the phosphorylation of SP1, regardless of the presence or absence of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C, D

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection prompted a redistribution of HNF4α from the nucleus to cytoplasm
source: SARS-CoV-2 infection prompted a redistribution of HNF4α from the nucleus to cytoplasm, while colchicine treatment induced its nuclear accumulation both in the presence and absence of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 2E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2E, F

claim: Treatment with MithA or knockdown of SP1 by siRNA down-regulated ACE2 protein expression in HPAEpiCs
source: First, western blot analysis demonstrated that treatment with MithA, a selective SP1 inhibitor, or knockdown of SP1 by small interfering RNA (siRNA) down-regulated ACE2 protein expression in HPAEpiCs (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A, B

claim: Treatment with the HNF4α antagonist BI6015 and knockdown of HNF4α by siRNA up-regulated ACE2 protein expression
source: In contrast, treatment with the HNF4α antagonist BI6015 and knockdown of HNF4α by siRNA up-regulated ACE2 protein expression (Figure 3C, D), which was blocked by colchicine administration.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C, D

claim: MithA treatment inhibited the protein expression of ACE2, but did not further reduce the expression of ACE2 suppressed by colchicine
source: Immunofluorescence staining further confirmed that although MithA treatment inhibited the protein expression of ACE2, it did not further reduce the expression of ACE2 suppressed by colchicine (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E, F

claim: Supplementation with BI6015 markedly increased the expression of ACE2 in HPAEpiCs, which was reduced by colchicine treatment
source: Supplementation with BI6015 markedly increased the expression of ACE2 in HPAEpiCs, which was reduced by colchicine treatment (Figure 3E, F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E, F

claim: MithA treatment inhibited luciferase activity of the ACE2 promoter, but not in the presence of colchicine
source: Based on a luciferase reporter gene containing the ACE2 promoter, MithA treatment inhibited luciferase activity, but not in the presence of colchicine (Figure 3G), while BI6015 treatment increased luciferase activity.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3G

claim: The binding of SP1 to the GC box of the ACE2 promoter was significantly reduced after colchicine treatment
source: In addition, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR analysis indicated that the binding of SP1 to the GC box of the ACE2 promoter was significantly reduced, while the binding of HNF4α to the AGGTCA element was markedly increased after colchicine treatment (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The binding of HNF4α to the AGGTCA element of the ACE2 promoter was markedly increased after colchicine treatment
source: In addition, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-qPCR analysis indicated that the binding of SP1 to the GC box of the ACE2 promoter was significantly reduced, while the binding of HNF4α to the AGGTCA element was markedly increased after colchicine treatment (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3H

claim: MithA inhibited SARS-CoV-2 replication in HPAEpiCs, with an EC50 value of 0.1948 μM
source: Results showed that MithA inhibited SARS-CoV-2 replication in HPAEpiCs, with an EC50 value of 0.1948 μM (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Treatment with the SP1 inhibitor MithA markedly suppressed SP1 phosphorylation
source: Interestingly, treatment with the SP1 inhibitor MithA markedly suppressed SP1 phosphorylation, whereas treatment with the HNF4α antagonist BI6015 increased SP1 phosphorylation at Thr453 (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: Treatment with the HNF4α antagonist BI6015 increased SP1 phosphorylation at Thr453
source: Interestingly, treatment with the SP1 inhibitor MithA markedly suppressed SP1 phosphorylation, whereas treatment with the HNF4α antagonist BI6015 increased SP1 phosphorylation at Thr453 (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: BI6015 induced the cytoplasmic translocation of HNF4α
source: In addition, BI6015 induced the cytoplasmic translocation of HNF4α, while MithA promoted its nuclear accumulation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C, D

claim: MithA promoted nuclear accumulation of HNF4α
source: In addition, BI6015 induced the cytoplasmic translocation of HNF4α, while MithA promoted its nuclear accumulation (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C, D

claim: Western blot analysis showed an elevation in SP1 phosphorylation levels following the knockdown of HNF4α by siRNA
source: Western blot analysis showed an elevation in SP1 phosphorylation levels following the knockdown of HNF4α by siRNA (Figure 4E, F), whereas the knockdown of SP1 had no discernible impact on the total levels of HNF4α.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E, F

claim: The knockdown of SP1 had no discernible impact on the total levels of HNF4α
source: Western blot analysis showed an elevation in SP1 phosphorylation levels following the knockdown of HNF4α by siRNA (Figure 4E, F), whereas the knockdown of SP1 had no discernible impact on the total levels of HNF4α.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4E, F

claim: Potential interactions between SP1 and HNF4α in HPAEpiCs were confirmed using co-immunoprecipitation assay
source: We subsequently confirmed potential interactions between SP1 and HNF4α in HPAEpiCs using co-immunoprecipitation assay (co-IP; Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4G

claim: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is activated by SARS-CoV-2 infection
source: The PI3K/AKT signaling pathway is reportedly activated by SARS-CoV-2 infection (Callahan et al., 2021; Klann et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and confirmed by experimental data in this study

claim: SARS-CoV-2 infection enhanced the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473 and Thr308
source: Consistently, we found that SARS-CoV-2 infection enhanced the phosphorylation of AKT at Ser473 and Thr308, which is required for its activation (Su et al., 2011; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A–C and a citation

claim: Colchicine treatment markedly reduced the phosphorylation of AKT induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection
source: However, treatment with colchicine markedly reduced the phosphorylation of AKT induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A–C

claim: Knockdown of AKT by siRNA or treatment with PI3K inhibitors (LY294002 and wortmannin) down-regulated the expression of ACE2 in HPAEpiCs
source: Furthermore, knockdown of AKT by siRNA or treatment with PI3K inhibitors (LY294002 and wortmannin) down-regulated the expression of ACE2 in HPAEpiCs (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5D–G

claim: LY294002 inhibited SARS-CoV-2 infection in HPAEpiCs, with an EC50 value of 0.2381 μM
source: Notably, both LY294002 and wortmannin inhibited SARS-CoV-2 infection in HPAEpiCs, with EC50 values of 0.2381 μM and 0.04228 μM, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Wortmannin inhibited SARS-CoV-2 infection in HPAEpiCs, with an EC50 value of 0.04228 μM
source: Notably, both LY294002 and wortmannin inhibited SARS-CoV-2 infection in HPAEpiCs, with EC50 values of 0.2381 μM and 0.04228 μM, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Activation of AKT promotes the stability and localization of SP1 by phosphorylating SP1 at Thr453 and Thr739
source: Activation of AKT promotes the stability and localization of SP1 by phosphorylating SP1 at Thr453 and Thr739 (Adapala et al., 2019; Gómez-Villafuertes et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015), and prevents the nuclear translocation of HNF4α (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: Activation of AKT prevents the nuclear translocation of HNF4α
source: Activation of AKT promotes the stability and localization of SP1 by phosphorylating SP1 at Thr453 and Thr739 (Adapala et al., 2019; Gómez-Villafuertes et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015), and prevents the nuclear translocation of HNF4α (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Suppression of AKT by siRNA or its inhibitors significantly reduced the accumulation of phospho-SP1 in the nucleus
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that suppression of AKT by siRNA or its inhibitors significantly reduced the accumulation of phospho-SP1 in the nucleus, but markedly promoted the nuclear translocation of HNF4α (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5H–K

claim: Suppression of AKT by siRNA or its inhibitors markedly promoted the nuclear translocation of HNF4α
source: Consistent with these observations, we found that suppression of AKT by siRNA or its inhibitors significantly reduced the accumulation of phospho-SP1 in the nucleus, but markedly promoted the nuclear translocation of HNF4α (Figure 5H–K).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5H–K

claim: The expression of ACE2 was significantly up-regulated in the lungs and trachea of hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2 compared to the non-infected control group
source: Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that the expression of ACE2 was significantly up-regulated in the lungs and trachea of hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2 compared to the non-infected control group (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: Colchicine or MithA treatment substantially inhibited the expression of ACE2 in both the lungs and trachea of hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2
source: However, colchicine or MithA treatment substantially inhibited the expression of ACE2 in both the lungs and trachea of hamsters infected with SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Treatment with colchicine or MithA reduced viral replication in both the lungs and trachea of hamsters
source: Based on immunofluorescence analysis of SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid and RT-qPCR, treatment with colchicine or MithA reduced viral replication in both the lungs and trachea of hamsters (Figure 6B–D; Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, D), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C, D

claim: Histopathological analysis of lung tissues 3 dpi revealed a range of pulmonary abnormalities, including bronchial epithelial cell necrosis and nuclear pyknosis, extensive alveolar hemorrhage, marked infiltration of inflammatory cells, significant edema, and notably thickened alveolar walls
source: Subsequent histopathological analysis of lung tissues 3 dpi revealed a range of pulmonary abnormalities, including bronchial epithelial cell necrosis and nuclear pyknosis, extensive alveolar hemorrhage, marked infiltration of inflammatory cells, significant edema, and notably thickened alveolar walls (Figure 6E, G).
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6E, G

claim: The severity of pathological features in the lungs was markedly reduced in the treatment groups compared to the mock group
source: Although similar pathological features were present, their severity was markedly reduced in the treatment groups compared to the mock group.
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 6E, G

claim: Collagen deposition indicative of fibrosis was evident in the lungs of infected hamsters
source: Using Masson's trichrome staining, collagen deposition indicative of fibrosis was evident in the lungs of infected hamsters (Figure 6F, H).
evidence: This is supported by Masson staining data shown in Figure 6F, H

claim: Treatment with either colchicine or MithA effectively reversed lung fibrosis
source: Of note, treatment with either colchicine or MithA effectively reversed lung fibrosis.
evidence: This is supported by Masson staining data shown in Figure 6F, H

claim: Acute kidney injury associated with severe SARS-CoV-2 serves as an independent risk factor for in-hospital death in patients
source: Although acute kidney injury associated with severe SARS-CoV-2 serves as an independent risk factor for in-hospital death in patients (Nadim et al., 2020), whether SARS-CoV-2 directly infects the kidney remains unclear (Smith and Akilesh, 2021; Wysocki et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Immunofluorescence analysis detected the substantial presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the kidneys of infected hamsters
source: Here, immunofluorescence analysis detected the substantial presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the kidneys of infected hamsters, an effect markedly mitigated by colchicine or MithA treatment (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A, B

claim: Colchicine or MithA treatment markedly mitigated the presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the kidneys of infected hamsters
source: Here, immunofluorescence analysis detected the substantial presence of SARS-CoV-2 in the kidneys of infected hamsters, an effect markedly mitigated by colchicine or MithA treatment (Figure 7A, B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A, B

claim: Both colchicine and MithA effectively down-regulated ACE2 expression in the kidneys of infected hamsters
source: Further analysis also showed that both drugs effectively down-regulated ACE2 expression (Figure 7C, D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C, D

claim: Histopathological evaluation showed significant renal damage in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters, including renal tubular epithelial cell nuclear pyknosis, brush border disappearance, renal interstitial vascular congestion, inflammatory cell infiltration, and glomerular atrophy
source: Histopathological evaluation showed significant renal damage in SARS-CoV-2-infected hamsters, including renal tubular epithelial cell nuclear pyknosis, brush border disappearance, renal interstitial vascular congestion, inflammatory cell infiltration, and glomerular atrophy (Figure 7E, F).
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 7E, F

claim: In the drug-treated hamsters, the glomeruli displayed uniform distribution and intact structure, tubular epithelial cells appeared normal, and brush borders showed neat arrangement, with no evident abnormality in the renal medulla or obvious hyperplasia in the renal interstitium
source: In the drug-treated hamsters, however, the glomeruli displayed uniform distribution and intact structure, tubular epithelial cells appeared normal, and brush borders showed neat arrangement, with no evident abnormality in the renal medulla or obvious hyperplasia in the renal interstitium.
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 7E, F

claim: Under physiological conditions, SP1 is primarily localized in the nucleus, while HNF4α exhibits a dual distribution in the nucleus and cytoplasm
source: Under physiological conditions, SP1 is primarily localized in the nucleus, while HNF4α exhibits a dual distribution in the nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from immunofluorescence data

claim: SP1 and HNF4α exert opposing effects on the regulation of ACE2 expression, thereby maintaining basal expression of ACE2
source: These transcription factors exert opposing effects on the regulation of ACE2 expression, thereby maintaining basal expression of ACE2.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing opposite regulatory effects

claim: Upon infection by SARS-CoV-2, the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway becomes activated
source: Upon infection by SARS-CoV-2, the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway becomes activated (Klann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by experimental data in this study

claim: Activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway promotes the transcriptional activity of SP1 through increased phosphorylation in the nucleus
source: This activation subsequently promotes the transcriptional activity of SP1 through increased phosphorylation in the nucleus and suppresses the transcriptional activity of HNF4α by inducing its translocation to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased SP1 phosphorylation and effects of AKT inhibition

claim: Activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway suppresses the transcriptional activity of HNF4α by inducing its translocation to the cytoplasm
source: This activation subsequently promotes the transcriptional activity of SP1 through increased phosphorylation in the nucleus and suppresses the transcriptional activity of HNF4α by inducing its translocation to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cytoplasmic translocation of HNF4α and effects of AKT inhibition

claim: Induction of ACE2 expression may represent a strategic adaptation of SARS-CoV-2 to facilitate its own propagation
source: Given that ACE2 serves as the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2, induction of ACE2 expression may represent a strategic adaptation of the virus to facilitate its own propagation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed up-regulation of ACE2 and its role as a viral receptor

claim: Phosphoproteomic analysis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cells has revealed the activation of the growth factor receptor (GFR) and its downstream pathways, including the RAF/MEK/ERK MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways
source: Phosphoproteomic analysis of SARS-CoV-2-infected cells has revealed the activation of the growth factor receptor (GFR) and its downstream pathways, including the RAF/MEK/ERK MAPK and PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathways, in SARS-CoV-2-infected cells (Klann et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Blockage of the GFR signaling pathway via application of prominent anti-cancer drugs effectively prevents SARS-CoV-2 replication in cellular models
source: Blockage of the GFR signaling pathway via application of prominent anti-cancer drugs, such as sorafenib (RAF inhibitor), RO5126766 (dual RAF/MEK inhibitor), pictilisib (PI3K inhibitor), and omipalisib (dual PI3K and mTOR inhibitor), effectively prevents SARS-CoV-2 replication in cellular models.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: The PI3K/AKT signaling cascade served as a crucial regulatory node in the induction of ACE2 expression by enhancing and reducing the transcriptional activities of SP1 and HNF4α, respectively
source: Notably, our findings indicated that the PI3K/AKT signaling cascade, activated following SARS-CoV-2 infection (Klann et al., 2020), served as a crucial regulatory node in the induction of ACE2 expression by enhancing and reducing the transcriptional activities of SP1 and HNF4α, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects of PI3K/AKT inhibition on SP1 and HNF4α activities

claim: Inhibition of SP1 activity, leading to the down-regulation of ACE2 expression, effectively mitigated SARS-CoV-2 replication in the lung and trachea of Syrian hamsters
source: Our findings also showed that inhibition of SP1 activity, leading to the down-regulation of ACE2 expression, effectively mitigated SARS-CoV-2 replication in the lung and trachea of Syrian hamsters.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data in Syrian hamsters

claim: The decrease in viral replication was associated with a marked reduction in lung pathology
source: Importantly, this decrease in viral replication was associated with a marked reduction in lung pathology.
evidence: This is supported by histopathological data from Syrian hamsters

claim: Acute kidney injury has been identified as an extrapulmonary manifestation of severe COVID-19
source: In addition to lung-associated issues, acute kidney injury has also been identified as an extrapulmonary manifestation of severe COVID-19 (Legrand et al., 2021), although the direct causal association between SARS-CoV-2 infection and acute kidney injury remains controversial (Legrand et al., 2021; Smith and Akilesh, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research

claim: SARS-CoV-2 can directly infect kidney cells in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney organoids
source: Recent evidence has indicated that SARS-CoV-2 can directly infect kidney cells in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived kidney organoids (Jansen et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Colchicine treatment effectively suppressed ACE2 expression in the proximal kidney tubule, which was associated with diminished SARS-CoV-2-induced kidney injury in Syrian hamsters
source: Consistent with these findings, we found that colchicine treatment effectively suppressed ACE2 expression in the proximal kidney tubule, which was associated with diminished SARS-CoV-2-induced kidney injury in Syrian hamsters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Syrian hamsters

claim: Proxalutamide, a potent androgen receptor antagonist, has been shown to suppress androgen-induced ACE2 expression
source: Notably, proxalutamide, a potent androgen receptor antagonist, has been shown to suppress androgen-induced ACE2 expression (Qiao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: RIPK1 inhibition has been found to reduce viral loads in SARS-CoV-2-infected human lung organoids, accompanied by a down-regulation in the transcriptional induction of ACE2
source: Moreover, RIPK1 inhibition has been found to reduce viral loads in SARS-CoV-2-infected human lung organoids, accompanied by a down-regulation in the transcriptional induction of ACE2 (Xu et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Inhibition of FXR activity via UDCA can lead to the down-regulation of ACE2 expression, consequently reducing SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo
source: A recent study also demonstrated that inhibition of FXR activity via UDCA can lead to the down-regulation of ACE2 expression, consequently reducing SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo (Brevini et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research

claim: Inhibition of SP1 by its inhibitor MithA induced nuclear accumulation of HNF4α
source: Notably, inhibition of SP1 by its inhibitor MithA induced nuclear accumulation of HNF4α, whereas inhibition of HNF4α by its antagonist BI6015 increased phosphorylation levels of SP1 in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence and western blot analyses

claim: Inhibition of HNF4α by its antagonist BI6015 increased phosphorylation levels of SP1 in the nucleus
source: Notably, inhibition of SP1 by its inhibitor MithA induced nuclear accumulation of HNF4α, whereas inhibition of HNF4α by its antagonist BI6015 increased phosphorylation levels of SP1 in the nucleus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from immunofluorescence and western blot analyses

claim: MithA is capable of inducing proteasome-dependent SP1 degradation
